questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Rewriting a claim so a reply can engage it
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a claim must specify before it can be replied to
questions.stem: In a clerk's file note, a client's letter says the landlord's notice was unreasonable. What must be done with the claim before the reply can engage it?

options.text: It must be restated so that it says precisely what was unreasonable and why.
It must be shortened, because long claims cannot be answered.
options.misconception: confuses rewriting for making a claim answerable with trimming it

options.text: It must be supported with photographs of the property.
options.misconception: assumes the problem is a lack of evidence

options.text: It must be withdrawn, because the client is unlikely to win the point.
options.misconception: turns a drafting task into a decision about the case

questions.explanation: A reply can only engage a claim it can identify. The clerk's job is to make the client's vague assertion into a proposition that can be agreed, disputed or tested.
questions.hint: Ask what the reply would have to answer.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a disagreement can arise from differing meanings
questions.stem: The client rejected the settlement because the offer was too low, but the other side's solicitor read that as a complaint about procedure. Explain how this disagreement arose.

answer.exemplar: The two accounts share a description of the settlement but attach different meanings to it. The client took the offer as a judgment on the value of the claim, while the other solicitor treated the rejection as a complaint about procedure, so each side was answering a different proposition under the same word. Clarifying which of the two the client meant would have removed the disagreement, or shown at once that it ran deeper than a miscommunication.

questions.explanation: Two parties can disagree because the same words describe different things for each of them. Naming which proposition was actually rejected distinguishes a miscommunication from a real conflict.
questions.hint: Ask what the word meant to each side.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose a reply that addressed a different question

stimulus.body: File note. A member of the tenants' group asked at the open session whether the proposed rent review would apply to existing leases. The solicitor's reply on file states that the review is scheduled for the autumn and applies to leases signed after that date. The note records that the group wrote again saying the reply had not answered their question.

questions.stem: From that note, what went wrong with the reply to the member?

options.text: It relied on a date that the group had not been told about.
options.misconception: assumes the mistake was withholding information

options.text: It addressed the question but in language the group found unhelpful.
options.misconception: treats a clarity problem as if it were a wrong answer

options.text: It answered a different question from the one the member had asked.
It should have been given orally rather than in writing.
options.misconception: picks a mode of reply rather than its content

questions.explanation: The member asked about existing leases and received an answer about future ones. The reply was about a different proposition, so it could not have satisfied the question however clearly it was put.
questions.hint: Compare the question with the reply.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether a closing formula records any undertaking
questions.stem: A closing in a file note read that the other side would review the position before responding. What does the note show about commitment?

options.text: A firm undertaking to reconsider the offer and reply.
options.misconception: reads a formulaic phrase as a firm undertaking

options.text: A refusal to engage with the offer at all.
options.misconception: treats a neutral phrase as a complete refusal

options.text: An agreement to meet the client's figure.
options.misconception: infers a concession from a procedural phrase

options.text: A formula that records no undertaking to answer or to act.

questions.explanation: The phrase is what gets written when nothing has been promised. Reading a closing as commitment requires evidence of what was actually agreed, not the presence of a courteous formula.
questions.hint: Ask what was actually undertaken.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A synthesis that only relocates the disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a synthesis that relocates rather than narrows a dispute
questions.stem: The parties' joint submission left the dispute about whether the delay was reasonable. Which observation describes that synthesis?

options.text: It restates the disagreement without changing what is at stake between the parties.
It narrows the dispute to a single question that can now be answered.
options.misconception: credits the synthesis with progress it did not make

options.text: It records an agreement on the facts and leaves only the law in dispute.
options.misconception: assumes a synthesis always produces a factual agreement

options.text: It closes the dispute by adopting a neutral position on the delay.
options.misconception: reads a restatement as an actual resolution

questions.explanation: A synthesis that only relocates a dispute leaves the parties exactly where they were, because no common ground has been established to argue from. The sign of a real synthesis is that the parties can now do something with the result.
questions.hint: Ask what the parties gained from it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Select the opening that states both sides of a disagreement
questions.stem: Which opening best names the disagreement in a clerk's file note about a disputed clause?

options.text: We have considered the matter and our position remains as set out.
options.misconception: repeats a position rather than naming the disagreement

options.text: The parties agree the clause is unclear but differ on how it should be read.
Please find our comments on the clause in draft four.
options.misconception: opens with an administrative note rather than the dispute

options.text: The clause should be redrafted in the form enclosed.
options.misconception: opens with an instruction rather than a disagreement

questions.explanation: An opening that names the disagreement shows what the parties share and where they diverge. Openings that repeat a position or pass papers leave the reader to work out what is actually in dispute.
questions.hint: Look for an opening that states both sides.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Counterarguments aimed at a nearby claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes a counterargument a move against relevance
questions.stem: A solicitor's submission argues that the tenant's complaint about the deposit is beside the point. Explain what makes an argument like that a counterargument aimed at a nearby claim.

answer.exemplar: The counterargument does not deny the deposit complaint; it argues that the complaint is beside the point, which is a move against its relevance rather than its truth. That is characteristic of an argument aimed at a nearby claim: it leaves the claim standing but shifts the ground so that the claim no longer counts for the purpose in hand. The danger is that the two claims are not quite adjacent, and defeating relevance is not the same as defeating the complaint.

questions.explanation: An argument aimed at a nearby claim disputes where the claim belongs rather than whether it is true. That distinction matters, because a complaint can be true and still irrelevant to the issue in hand.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of objection is being made.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Rewriting a claim so a reply can engage it
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a claim must contain before it can be answered

stimulus.body: File note. The client wrote: the survey is useless and the buyer has no right to rely on it. Instructing solicitor's reply on file states that the survey was prepared to the agreed standard and that a reliance provision is proposed in draft five. The note records the client as not having replied to draft five.

questions.stem: According to the note, what did the client's claim need before it could be answered?

options.text: A rewording that makes the complaint sound less strong.
options.misconception: treats rewriting as tone management

options.text: An explanation of why the survey was prepared to that standard.
options.misconception: assumes the claim needs a defence rather than a specification

options.text: A decision about whether to rely on the survey at all.
options.misconception: turns a drafting step into a strategic decision

options.text: A statement of what is wrong with the survey and what remedy is wanted.

questions.explanation: The client asserted that the survey was useless, which the solicitor's reply could not meet because it did not say on what ground or with what remedy. Stating the defect and the remedy is what would make the claim answerable.
questions.hint: Ask what the reply would need to address.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Classify a disagreement that turns on differing meanings
questions.stem: One side described the payment as part of the consideration and the other recorded it as a payment on account. What kind of disagreement is this?

options.text: A disagreement in meaning that would disappear once the term is agreed.
A disagreement about the law that has no shared vocabulary at all.
options.misconception: dismisses the shared wording instead of the shared meaning

options.text: A genuine conflict of interest that no wording could resolve.
options.misconception: assumes the parties' interests rather than their words are the problem

options.text: A disagreement that has been resolved by the clerk's file note.
options.misconception: claims a resolution the note does not record

questions.explanation: Both sides used terms of payment but attached different consequences to them, which is a disagreement in meaning rather than in substance. Agreeing what the payment is would settle the point without either side conceding its interest.
questions.hint: Ask what the same words are doing for each side.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Select the reply that gives a member the position asked for
questions.stem: A member asks whether the case will be settled before the hearing. Which reply actually answers the member?

options.text: The matter is listed for a hearing in March, which is the current position.
options.misconception: supplies a related fact without answering the question

options.text: No date for settlement has been agreed, and a settlement would have to be approved by both sides.
Settlement is possible in principle if the parties continue to discuss it.
options.misconception: leaves the member without the position on timing

options.text: The question of settlement will be dealt with at the hearing.
options.misconception: defers the answer to a point where it is less useful

questions.explanation: The member asked about timing, and the answer gives the actual position: no date has been agreed and what a settlement would require. A related fact or a general possibility does not tell the member where things stand.
questions.hint: Ask whether the member learns the position.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: State what a closing about reporting commits the other side to
questions.stem: In a file note, the other side's solicitor wrote that they would revert once their client had considered the offer. What does the closing commit the other side to?

options.text: To accepting the offer if their client approves it.
options.misconception: reads the closing as an undertaking on the substance

options.text: To reporting back whether the client approves the offer.
options.misconception: overreads a procedural step as a substantive undertaking

options.text: Only to coming back with an answer, not to any particular answer.
Nothing, since the offer was made without prejudice and binds nobody.
options.misconception: rules out any commitment because of the without prejudice status

questions.explanation: The undertaking is to respond, and the content of that response is left open. A closing that refers back to a client fixes the obligation to report, not the obligation to accept.
questions.hint: Ask what the closing actually promises.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A synthesis that only relocates the disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a reframing may not narrow a dispute
questions.stem: The parties agree that the issue is not the delay but the notification of it. Explain why this may not be the progress it appears to be.

answer.exemplar: Moving the dispute from the delay to the notification only works if the parties are now in agreement about what the notification ought to have been, because otherwise they have simply taken the same argument and moved it one step along. A check worth making is whether anything has been accepted that was not accepted before. If not, the note has relocated the disagreement without narrowing it, and the work of arguing has only been deferred.

questions.explanation: Relocating a dispute produces progress only if something has been agreed at the new location. Without that, the same disagreement has simply been moved one step along.
questions.hint: Ask what has been agreed that was not agreed before.

questions.learningObjective: Improve an opening so that it identifies the dispute

stimulus.body: File note. Instructing solicitor's opening paragraph: we write to address the points raised in the letter of 3 June, and to confirm the basis on which our client's account is set out. No summary of the dispute appears in the note.

questions.stem: On the face of the note, which improvement would make the opening name the disagreement?

options.text: Adding a sentence stating what the parties agree and where they differ.
Removing the reference to the letter of 3 June.
options.misconception: suggests the reference is what prevents the dispute being named

options.text: Adding a paragraph setting out the full background of the matter.
options.misconception: assumes the problem is too little background

options.text: Quoting the client's account in full at the start.
options.misconception: adds detail rather than identifying the dispute

questions.explanation: The opening as drafted says what the letter does but not what the dispute is. One sentence giving the common ground and the point of difference would tell the reader immediately what the letter has to answer.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader cannot tell from the note.

questions.topic: Counterarguments aimed at a nearby claim
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a relevance objection from a denial of the claim
questions.stem: A submission argues that the tenant's complaint about the condition of the flat is irrelevant because the tenant had not given notice. Which assessment is right?

options.text: It answers the complaint, because notice is a condition of any claim.
options.misconception: treats a relevance point as if it denied the complaint

options.text: It attacks the claim's place in the argument rather than its truth.
It is a counterargument to a different claim, so it should be ignored.
options.misconception: dismisses a relevant argument rather than weighing it

options.text: It proves the flat was in good condition throughout the tenancy.
options.misconception: reads a procedural objection as evidence about the condition

questions.explanation: The objection says the complaint does not count here, not that the complaint is untrue. That is a move against the claim's relevance, which is why it must be matched with an answer about the notice.
questions.hint: Ask whether the truth of the complaint is disputed.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Rewriting a claim so a reply can engage it
questions.learningObjective: Rewrite a general complaint into a specified claim
questions.stem: A client's instruction says the works were not done properly. Which rewrite makes the claim answerable?

options.text: The works were not done properly, and the client considers that a breach.
options.misconception: adds a legal label without saying what went wrong

options.text: The works were done badly, in a manner the client disputes.
options.misconception: changes the wording without identifying what is disputed

options.text: The works did not follow the agreed specification, in the respect of the drainage.
The client wishes the works to be inspected again before anything else happens.
options.misconception: substitutes a remedy for the claim being made

questions.explanation: The rewrite says what was required, what was done instead, and in which particular respect, so a reply can address it point by point. The alternatives either add a conclusion or drop the substance.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Identify a divergence in meaning between two records
questions.stem: In a file note, one side recorded that the sum was without prejudice and the other recorded that the sum was payable. What does this show?

options.text: One side has made a concession on the payment of the sum.
options.misconception: reads a label about the status of an offer as an agreement to pay

options.text: The parties disagree about how the sum was calculated.
options.misconception: supplies a substantive dispute the labels do not raise

options.text: The file note records the dispute in a way that favours one side.
options.misconception: supposes the note is partisan rather than ambiguous

options.text: A difference in what the parties understand the recorded sum to mean.

questions.explanation: One label describes the protection attached to an offer and the other treats it as a debt. Until the parties know which description governs, they cannot tell whether the sum is being offered or claimed.
questions.hint: Ask what each label is doing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an answer to a member must contain
questions.stem: A member of the residents' association asks whether the repairs will be done before the winter. Explain what an answer to that question must contain.

answer.exemplar: The member is asking about a date and a sequence, so an answer has to give the position on both: whether the work is scheduled before the winter, and if it is not, what is scheduled instead and when. A reply that acknowledges the concern and promises attention tells the member nothing they can rely on, because there is no position against which the reply can later be checked, and the question remains outstanding on the file in substance.

questions.explanation: An answer must give the position on the point asked, so that it can be relied on and later checked. An acknowledgement of the concern leaves the question open in substance.
questions.hint: Ask what the member could rely on.

questions.learningObjective: Read a closing for the undertaking it actually contains

options.misconception: reads a commitment to report as a commitment to a particular answer

options.text: Only to getting back in touch about those points.

options.misconception: rules out a procedural undertaking because of the letter's status

options.text: To a meeting between the parties before any further correspondence.
options.misconception: invents a commitment to a meeting that the letter does not mention

questions.explanation: The undertaking is to come back about the points raised. Nothing in the letter ties the sender to a position, a meeting or a date, so a commitment has to be read from what was actually promised.
questions.hint: Ask what the letter actually promises.

options.misconception: describes the document rather than the disagreement

questions.topic: Counterarguments aimed at a nearby claim
questions.learningObjective: Define a counterargument aimed at a nearby claim
questions.stem: What distinguishes a counterargument aimed at a nearby claim from one aimed at the claim itself?

options.text: It attacks the standing or relevance of the claim rather than its truth.
It deals with a claim that is worded differently but means the same thing.
options.misconception: confuses a nearby claim with a differently worded one

options.text: It quotes the claim back before disputing it, which shows the writer is careful.
options.misconception: mistakes quotation for the substance of the move

options.text: It is raised after the main argument rather than before it.
options.misconception: treats the order of presentation as the distinguishing feature

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Rewriting a claim so a reply can engage it
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an instruction must be rewritten before it is sent
questions.stem: An instruction in the file records that the client was unfairly treated. Explain why this instruction has to be rewritten before it can be sent as a claim.

answer.exemplar: As drafted, the instruction asserts a conclusion about fairness without identifying the act complained of, the harm it caused, or the remedy sought, so the other side would have to guess which of several possible claims is being made. A usable version would say what was done, when, by whom, what the client says followed from it, and what the client wants done about it. Each element gives the reply something specific to accept, dispute or answer.

questions.explanation: A claim has to name what happened and what is wanted, otherwise a reply can only guess at its target. Rewriting supplies the elements a reply can be addressed to.
questions.hint: Ask what a reply would have to answer.

options.misconception: supplies a financial dispute the note does not mention

options.text: A disagreement about which party must perform first under the agreement.
options.misconception: supposes a sequencing dispute the note does not raise

A disagreement about whether the agreement was ever signed at all.
options.misconception: invents an issue about the agreement's existence

questions.explanation: One record describes declining to renew and the other describes declining to extend, and the tenant drew a further conclusion from the first. That is a divergence in meaning between the two descriptions, which can be closed by asking what each party meant.

options.misconception: describes a narrowing that has not happened

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a summary must include to name a disagreement
questions.stem: A clerk's file note summarises a call: we discussed the repair costs and the other side said the amount was excessive. Explain why this summary does not name the disagreement.

answer.exemplar: The summary records a topic and an adjective, but it does not say what the other side was comparing the cost against, or what it was claiming the cost should have been. Without that, a reader cannot tell whether the parties differ about the price of the works or about who was quoted for them, and the dispute cannot be framed for either side to answer. Naming the disagreement means giving the point of difference, not a characterisation of one side's tone.

questions.explanation: A summary that says one side called a figure excessive leaves out what the figure was being compared against. Naming the disagreement requires the point of difference, not a characterisation.
questions.hint: Ask what the figure was being compared with.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a relevance objection that leaves the complaint standing

options.misconception: turns a relevance objection into a dispute about the inspection

questions.hint: Ask whether the truth of the complaint is in issue.

questions.stem: A client's draft says the landlord was negligent. Which rewrite makes the claim answerable?

options.text: The landlord failed to repair the roof after notice in March, and the ceiling collapsed in May.
The landlord's handling of the roof repair was negligent and below the standard expected.
options.misconception: adds a standard of care without saying what was done

options.text: The landlord's negligence in the roof repair should be compensated as a breach of duty.
options.misconception: turns a factual claim into a legal conclusion

options.text: The landlord should be asked to explain the state of the roof before the hearing.
options.misconception: replaces the claim with a request for information

questions.explanation: The rewrite gives the duty that was owed, the failure, and the resulting harm, so each of those can be accepted, disputed or explained. A characterisation without facts gives the other side nothing to answer.
questions.hint: Ask what a reply would have to address.

questions.learningObjective: Select the question that tests a shared meaning
questions.stem: A file note records that one side asked for the balance outstanding and the other replied with a figure for the amount due. Which reply would best test whether the two are using the words the same way?

options.misconception: confirms the figure without testing the meaning of the words

options.text: Do you mean the sum claimed as unpaid, or the sum due under the agreement?
We have provided the balance as requested and note your figure differs.
options.misconception: records the discrepancy without resolving what it turns on

options.text: Our figure is correct and supported by the correspondence of 4 April.
options.misconception: asserts the rightness of one figure rather than testing the terms

questions.explanation: The question offers the two candidate meanings and asks which is meant, which is what surfaces a divergence between the parties without either conceding its position.
questions.hint: Ask which of two meanings applies.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a promise to consider is not a promise to accept
questions.stem: A closing in a file note recorded that the other side would consider the client's final position and revert. Explain why this is not a commitment to accept the offer.

answer.exemplar: The undertaking is to consider the position and to come back, and the consideration of the offer is left at the other side's discretion, which is precisely what was reserved. Nothing in the phrase ties the other side to a favourable outcome, so the file must record a reporting obligation and nothing more. Reading it as acceptance would put the clerk's note at odds with the words that were actually used, and would mislead whoever relies on the note later.

questions.explanation: A commitment to consider is a commitment to report back, not to agree. Recording it as acceptance would misstate the words actually used.
questions.hint: Ask what was reserved to the other side.

It has agreed the sum, leaving only the form of the payment open.
options.misconception: claims an agreement on the figure the note does not record

options.text: It has removed the delay from the dispute entirely and left the parties in agreement.
options.misconception: treats an issue set aside as a point resolved

options.text: It has settled the matter, since only one question now remains open.
options.misconception: confuses a single question with a resolved dispute

questions.explanation: Setting the delay aside and restating the dispute as a question of the sum has not resolved the money question, which is now the whole of the dispute. Nothing has been agreed on the new ground, so the parties are still arguing about the same sum.

options.misconception: adds a detail without saying what is being claimed

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Explain why labelling positions as the same conceals a dispute
questions.stem: A file note records the parties' positions as the same, when the entries in fact show one asked for a fixed fee and the other offered an hourly rate. Explain what this shows.

answer.exemplar: Calling the positions the same hides the disagreement rather than resolving it, and the two entries are not the same position at all: one is a proposal about how the work is priced and the other is a proposal about what the work should cost. Recording them as agreement risks the file suggesting a concession that nobody made, and it hides the point on which an actual bargain could be struck, which is how the engagement would be structured rather than what it costs.

questions.explanation: Labelling two different positions as the same conceals the disagreement and may create a record of a concession nobody made. The notes must be set out in full so the difference can be worked on.
questions.hint: Ask what the two entries actually propose.

options.misconception: supplies a fact nobody has established about the subcommittee

options.text: An assessment of whether a member here has an interest in the outcome.
A statement of the deadline for bringing an appeal.
options.misconception: supplies a procedural detail instead of the answer asked for

options.text: Confirmation that the subcommittee was properly constituted.
options.misconception: answers a different question about the subcommittee rather than about the appeal

questions.explanation: The condition for an appeal is an interest in the outcome, so the answer to the member's question turns on whether such an interest exists here. The reply set out the rule and stopped, leaving the member with a rule and no application of it.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be checked for the rule to apply.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Counterarguments aimed at a nearby claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a standing objection must be answered on its own ground
questions.stem: A file note records a submission that says the tenant's argument on the deposit should not be pursued because the tenant has signed a release. Explain why this needs an answer about the release rather than about the deposit.

answer.exemplar: The submission does not deny that the deposit was wrongly withheld; it says the claim should not be pursued at all because of the release. That is an argument about the standing of the claim, and it is answered by examining whether the release covers this claim and was properly executed, not by disputing the underlying complaint. Treating it as a complaint about the deposit would concede the only point in issue and leave the real defence untouched.

questions.explanation: A counterargument aimed at a nearby claim shifts the ground on which the claim counts. Answering it requires addressing that ground, not the claim it steps around.
questions.hint: Ask what the submission says the claim cannot do.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A synthesis that only relocates the disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an agreement on procedure is not a synthesis
questions.stem: A file note records a conference at which the parties agreed to write to their clients and then to settle the dispute on the basis to be advised. Explain why this is not a synthesis.

answer.exemplar: The conference produced an agreement about what to do next, which is a step in the procedure rather than an agreement about the dispute. Nothing has been settled on the substance, and no ground has been agreed on which the parties could build, so the disagreement is still open in full. Treating a procedural agreement as a synthesis would leave the file suggesting that the matter is closer to resolution than it is, and would obscure the work that remains.

questions.explanation: Agreeing a next step is not an agreement about the dispute. Calling it a synthesis makes the file overstate how far the matter has advanced.
questions.hint: Ask what was agreed about the substance.

questions.topic: Rewriting a claim so a reply can engage it
questions.learningObjective: Set out what a draft complaint must establish before it is sent
questions.stem: A clerk is told to draft a claim that the surveyor's report is unreliable. Explain what the draft has to establish before it is sent.

answer.exemplar: The draft has to say what part of the report is said to be unreliable and on what basis, since a general complaint about a document gives the other side nothing to answer and invites a reply about the document as a whole. It should identify the particular figure, method or conclusion that is challenged, state the reason, and set out what the client seeks to be done about it. Only then can the surveyor or the party relying on the report meet the point.

questions.explanation: A complaint about a document in general cannot be replied to point by point. The draft must isolate what is challenged, why, and what is wanted.
questions.hint: Ask what part of the report is challenged.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Read a difference in description as a possible divergence of meaning

stimulus.body: File note. The landlord's agent wrote that the tenant had abandoned the flat by failing to respond to letters. The tenant's clerk wrote that the tenant had not replied to letters of a particular date. The note records that the agent's letters had been sent to the address in the old tenancy agreement.

questions.stem: What does the difference in description suggest, on the note's account?

options.text: That the tenant had in fact abandoned the flat.
options.misconception: takes the agent's stronger word as the established position

options.text: That the two accounts of the tenant's conduct may not match.
That the tenant is relying on a technicality in the service of the letters.
options.misconception: supposes a defence the note does not record

options.text: That the agent's letters were not sent at all.
options.misconception: draws a delivery conclusion the note does not support

questions.explanation: One account uses a word that asserts an intention to give up the tenancy, and the other describes a failure to answer particular letters. That difference may reflect a difference in what each side believes happened, and it has to be settled before the word can carry any weight.
questions.hint: Ask what each word is being made to do.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Answer a member with the standard that applies to their case
questions.stem: A member asks whether the society's insurance covers damage to a home after a flood. Which reply actually answers?

options.text: Members should check their own policies as well as the society's cover.
options.misconception: gives advice without stating the position on the cover

options.text: Flood damage is covered, provided the policy was in force at the time.
options.misconception: states a general rule without connecting it to the member's case

options.text: The policy covers damage caused by escape of water, so a claim would be decided on that basis.
Claims of this kind are usually settled quickly by the insurers.
options.misconception: appeals to what is typical rather than to what the policy says

questions.explanation: The member asked what the cover is, and the reply says what the policy covers and how the claim would be judged. A general assurance or an appeal to usual practice leaves the member without the standard that applies to them.
questions.hint: Ask what the policy actually covers.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Record a review as a review and not as an acceptance
questions.stem: An entry in the file records that the other side's offer was under review and would be answered after the internal meeting. Which assessment is right?

options.text: The other side has undertaken to respond on a date to be fixed.
options.misconception: supplies a timetable the note does not record

options.text: The other side has accepted the offer in principle pending the meeting.
options.misconception: reads a review as an acceptance in principle

options.text: The other side has undertaken to recommend the offer to its client.
options.misconception: supplies an internal step the note does not mention

options.text: Only a statement that the offer is being considered and no more.

questions.explanation: The closing says the offer is under consideration and that a response will follow the internal meeting. Nothing is promised about the content of that response, so the file should record a review and a promise to reply, and no more.
questions.hint: Ask what the closing reserved to the other side.
